analogy.p: Imagine a pan of kernels popping at random. You cannot predict which kernel will pop next, yet the number popping each second follows a smooth pattern, and the time for half the unpopped kernels to pop is the same whether you start with a thousand or ten. Each 'pop' is like a decay, and the unpopped kernels are the unstable nuclei, so the rate falls as fewer remain. It breaks down because kernels pop partly because of heat, whereas radioactive decay is not affected by temperature at all.
analogy.t: A sack of popcorn kernels in a hot pan

bullets: **Random** means the decay of an individual nucleus cannot be predicted and is not affected by what neighbouring nuclei do.
Each nucleus has the same chance of decaying in any given time, regardless of how long it has already existed.
Decay is not affected by temperature, pressure, chemical reactions or physical state, because it is a nuclear process.
With a large number of nuclei the pattern becomes smooth and predictable; with very few nuclei the decay looks irregular.
Because of the randomness, repeated count rate readings fluctuate slightly around an average, so scientists take repeats and average them.
The randomness is why we need a statistical idea like half-life rather than a simple 'it will decay at 3 pm'.
This idea links directly to the uncertainty of experimental readings with a Geiger-Muller tube.
core.p: An unstable nucleus can emit radiation at any moment, and **radioactive decay is a random process**. This means that it is impossible to predict when one particular nucleus will decay, and two identical nuclei sitting side by side may decay at completely different times. What we CAN do is predict what happens to a very large number of nuclei, because the random events average out into a smooth, predictable pattern. This is exactly like tossing a coin: you cannot predict one toss, but you can say that about half of a thousand tosses will be heads.

bullets: Definition 1: time for the **number of nuclei** of the isotope in a sample to halve.
Definition 2: time for the **count rate** (or **activity**) from a sample to fall to half its initial level.
Half-life is a fixed property of each isotope; it is the same whatever the size of the sample.
Half-life does NOT mean that the whole sample has gone after two half-lives; it means half of what is left decays in each half-life.
Half-lives range from fractions of a second to billions of years depending on the isotope.
The word 'half' applies to the number of remaining (undecayed) nuclei, not to the mass of the whole sample, because the daughter products stay in the sample.
Always say 'the time taken for' in your definition; just 'when half has decayed' loses the time idea.
core.p: The **half-life** of a radioactive isotope is the **time it takes for the number of nuclei of the isotope in a sample to halve**. The specification gives an equivalent definition: the half-life is the **time it takes for the count rate (or activity) from a sample containing the isotope to fall to half its initial level**. Both definitions work because the count rate is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei still present. You must be able to quote both versions, and the mark scheme accepts either.

bullets: **Activity**: the rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays; measured in **becquerel, Bq**.
1 Bq = 1 decay per second.
**Count rate**: the number of decays recorded by a detector per unit time (counts per second or counts per minute).
A **Geiger-Muller tube** detects ionising radiation and a counter records the clicks.
The detector catches only a fraction of the radiation because it emits in all directions and some is absorbed on the way.
Because count rate is proportional to activity, a halving of one is a halving of the other.
Units: count rate is quoted as counts/s or counts/min; do not confuse it with the unit becquerel, which is used for activity.
core.p: Two related quantities appear in half-life questions. The **activity** of a source is the **rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays**, and it is measured in **becquerel (Bq)**, where 1 Bq is one decay per second. The **count rate** is the number of decays **recorded** per second or per minute by a detector such as a **Geiger-Muller tube**. The count rate is always smaller than the activity because the detector only catches the fraction of radiation that reaches it. The two are proportional, so both halve in one half-life.

bullets: Start: 1 (all). After 1 half-life: 1/2. After 2: 1/4. After 3: 1/8. After 4: 1/16. After 5: 1/32.
The amount lost is large at first (when many nuclei are available) and small later (when few remain).
The curve never quite reaches zero, because half of something is never nothing, although it becomes tiny.
The fraction remaining after n half-lives is (1/2) to the power n, i.e. 1 divided by 2^n.
The decay curve always has the same shape whatever the isotope; only the time scale changes.
The shape is decided by chance (random decay) plus the fact that fewer nuclei means fewer decays.
The same halving pattern applies to the activity and the count rate.
core.h: Why the number of nuclei halves each half-life (the exponential pattern)
core.p: In every half-life, **half of the nuclei still unchanged decay**. In the first half-life, half of the original number decays, leaving one half. In the next half-life, half of THAT decays, leaving one quarter, and so on. The pattern is therefore a halving each time, not a fixed number lost each time. This produces the typical curve that starts steep and gets shallower, called an **exponential decay curve**. The reason it flattens is that there are fewer unstable nuclei left to decay, so the activity is smaller.

bullets: Step 1: read the starting count rate (or activity) at time 0.
Step 2: divide it by 2 to find the half value.
Step 3: draw a horizontal line across at that value until it meets the curve, then go down to the time axis and read the time.
Step 4: that time is the half-life (if the start was at time 0).
Step 5: check by repeating from the half value to a quarter; the time interval should be the same.
Show construction lines on the graph; examiners often award a mark for them.
If the curve starts at a time other than zero, subtract the two times; do not just quote the later time.
Take care with the scale of the axes: count the squares or divisions carefully.
core.p: You are expected to **determine the half-life from a graph or a table**. The method is always the same: read the initial value, work out half of it, find the time at which the graph reaches half, and subtract the starting time. Good practice is to check with a second halving, for example from half to quarter, because the time for each halving should be identical; if it is not, you have misread the graph. This checking step is a typical way to earn the accuracy mark.

bullets: Find half of the starting value and look for it in the table.
If the exact half value is missing, plot the data and draw a smooth curve.
Check consistency: successive halving times should be (almost) equal.
Because of random variation, real readings scatter, so a best-fit smooth curve is better than joining dots.
Always subtract background count rate from every reading before looking for halving.
The first reading may not be at zero time; use differences in time.
Quote the half-life with units (seconds, minutes, hours, days or years).
core.h: Using a table of data to find half-life
core.p: A table of time and count rate can be used in the same way. Look for the value that is half the initial one; if it is not exactly listed, estimate between neighbouring readings or draw the graph. A table with constant halving intervals shows an exponential decay. If the data also include **background radiation** you must subtract it first, because the half-life applies only to the radiation from the source, not to the background, which does not decay in the same way.

bullets: After 1 half-life: remaining fraction 1/2; ratio initial : final = 2 : 1.
After 2 half-lives: 1/4; ratio 4 : 1.
After 3 half-lives: 1/8; ratio 8 : 1.
After 4 half-lives: 1/16; ratio 16 : 1.
After 5 half-lives: 1/32; ratio 32 : 1.
Fraction that has DECAYED after 3 half-lives = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8.
General: remaining = initial divided by 2^n.
If the question says 'ratio', give it as two numbers separated by a colon, e.g. 1 : 8, and state which way round it is.
core.h: Net decline after a number of half-lives (Higher tier)
core.p: **Higher tier only:** you must be able to **calculate the net decline, expressed as a ratio, in a radioactive emission after a given number of half-lives**. After n half-lives, the original is divided by 2 to the power n. So after 1 half-life the activity is 1/2 of the start, after 2 it is 1/4, after 3 it is 1/8. Expressed as a ratio of final to initial the answer is 1 : 2^n (equivalently initial : final is 2^n : 1). The 'net decline' is the overall fall, so state what is being compared clearly in the answer.

bullets: Number of half-lives = total time elapsed divided by the half-life.
Halve the starting value once for each half-life that has passed.
Example: 800 counts/min with half-life 10 min: after 30 min = 3 half-lives: 800 -> 400 -> 200 -> 100.
To find half-life from two values: count the halvings (e.g. 1200 -> 600 -> 300 -> 150 is 3 halvings) and divide the time by 3.
Make sure the time unit of the total time matches the half-life unit before dividing.
Show the halving in a chain; it is quicker, and shows method for the marks.
If the number of half-lives is not a whole number, read the answer from the graph instead (a non-whole number of half-lives is not asked as an exact calculation at GCSE).
core.p: Most half-life calculations are solved by **repeated halving**. First work out how many half-lives have passed by dividing the total time by the half-life. If this is a whole number, halve the starting value that many times. If you are asked to find the half-life from before and after values, count how many times you need to halve the start to get the end, then divide the total time by that number. There is no need to use logarithms at GCSE.

bullets: **Corrected count rate = measured count rate - background count rate**.
Measure background with the source removed; take repeats and an average.
If the background is not removed the half-life will be wrongly calculated, especially late on, when the source count rate is small.
Background does not halve; it stays roughly constant.
Example: measured 420 counts/min with background 20 counts/min gives corrected 400 counts/min.
Random fluctuations make small count rates less reliable than large ones.
The half-life of a source is a property of the source, so background must be removed to find it.
core.h: Background radiation and corrected count rate
core.p: A Geiger-Muller tube also detects **background radiation**, which comes from natural sources such as rocks, cosmic rays and from man-made sources like medical procedures. If you want the count rate from the source alone you must subtract the background count rate from your measured reading. The background does not decay with the sample's half-life, so failing to correct for it makes the half-life appear wrong. Measure the background first, with the source far away, and take an average.

bullets: **Short half-life**: high activity at first, but safe quickly; good for medical tracers because it does not stay in the body.
**Long half-life**: low activity now, but stays dangerous for a very long time; a problem for nuclear waste.
Smoke alarms use americium-241 with a very long half-life (hundreds of years) so they last, and emit alpha that is stopped in air.
Technetium-99m has a half-life of about 6 hours: long enough to scan, short enough to disappear.
Radioactive waste with a long half-life must be stored safely for thousands of years.
Isotopes with half-life of billions of years are used to date rocks.
Quoting the half-life without the idea of 'time' and 'use' will limit marks.
core.h: Short and long half-lives: what they mean
core.p: The size of the half-life tells you how quickly the radioactivity of a sample dies away and how long it stays dangerous. A **short half-life** means the nuclei decay quickly, so the source is very active at first but soon becomes harmless. A **long half-life** means the source stays radioactive for a long time but has a low activity at any moment. The best isotope for a job depends on this, and you must be able to give reasons that combine the length of the half-life with the use.

bullets: Measure the background count rate first with the source far away and take an average.
Place the source at a fixed distance from the GM tube so the fraction detected stays constant.
Record the count at regular time intervals, and repeat each reading, calculating a mean.
Subtract the background from each reading to find the corrected count rate.
Plot corrected count rate against time and draw a smooth best-fit curve.
Read off the time for the count rate to halve, and check with a second halving.
Safety: handle the source with tongs, keep it as far away as practical, store it in a lead-lined box when not in use, and keep exposure time short.
core.h: Practical: investigating decay with a Geiger-Muller tube
core.p: Although there is no required practical for half-life in the AQA GCSE physics list, you may be asked how to measure it or how to improve an experiment. A Geiger-Muller tube and counter record the count rate at regular time intervals, and the results are plotted as a graph. Because decay is random, the readings scatter, so repeats and long counting periods improve accuracy. Safety is a major part of the method.

bullets: Short half-life isotopes injected as tracers do little long-term harm because they die away quickly.
Long half-life isotopes inside the body would irradiate the tissue for years.
Waste from nuclear power must be kept safe for as long as the longest half-life isotopes remain active.
Use the type of radiation together with the half-life to choose isotopes for a use.
Sterilising equipment uses gamma with a half-life that is long enough to be practical.
Medical uses: the source must be a gamma emitter with a short half-life so it can leave the body in the organs scanned.
Half-life also explains why a sample of an old isotope is much less active than a fresh one.
core.p: Half-life ties into the safety topics. The half-life of an isotope decides how long a contaminated object or a nuclear waste product remains a hazard, and it helps in choosing isotopes for medical use. If an isotope is taken into the body (**contamination**), a short half-life means the radiation dose is quickly over, while a long half-life would give a long dose. An emitter of alpha is most dangerous inside the body, while outside the body gamma is the more penetrating.

bullets: Link to nuclear equations: they show WHAT the parent decays into; half-life shows HOW QUICKLY.
Link to maths: repeated halving is the same as multiplying by 1/2 each time (exponential decay).
Link to uncertainty: random decay means readings scatter; repeats improve reliability.
Always include units for time (s, min, h, days, years).
When reading values from a graph, use a ruler and construction lines, and state the values read.
Do not say 'it takes twice as long to finish' after 2 half-lives; it is a quarter left, not nothing.
For 6-mark questions, link the isotope's half-life, radiation type, and the use or hazard in a clear logical chain.
core.h: Link to other topics and common graph and exam skills
core.p: Half-life connects physics skills of graph reading, ratios and proportional reasoning. It is a standard source of data-handling questions in Paper 1 and uses the same skills as exponential change in maths. Remember that in exams the question will often give the half-life or show the graph, and your job is to read it carefully, show working and include units. The nuclear equation tells you what is formed; the half-life tells you how fast.

exam: Definition questions (1-2 marks): give 'time taken for' plus 'number of nuclei' or 'count rate/activity' and 'to halve / fall to half its initial level'.
Graph reading (2-3 marks): 1 mark for halving the initial value, 1 for reading the time, 1 for correct units; show construction lines.
Calculation (2-3 marks): work out the number of half-lives, show each halving, give the answer with units.
Higher tier ratio questions: 'net decline' after n half-lives is 2^n : 1 (initial : final); state which way round you give it.
Always check which quantity is asked: the amount remaining, the fraction decayed, or the ratio.
Background correction: if a question gives background, subtract it before halving; this is often the hidden mark.
Explain 'random' as: you cannot predict which nucleus will decay or when.
Model phrase: 'Half of the unstable nuclei decay in each half-life, so the count rate halves every half-life.'
4-mark questions often ask you to choose an isotope: link half-life (short or long), type of radiation and the use.
6-mark questions: structure the answer logically: what is the half-life, what does the data show, what does that mean for safety or use.
Practical questions: mention background, repeats and a mean, fixed distance, long counting time and safe handling.
Make sure graph axes are labelled with quantity and unit if you are asked to draw a decay curve; draw a smooth curve through the points, not dot to dot.

mistakes.r: After two half-lives one quarter of the original unstable nuclei remain.
mistakes.w: After two half-lives all the radioactive nuclei have gone.

mistakes.r: Half-life is the time for the number of nuclei (or count rate or activity) to fall to half its initial value.
mistakes.w: Half-life is the time for the sample to be half used up (vague).

mistakes.r: The curve never reaches zero; measure the time to fall to half of the starting value.
mistakes.w: Taking the half-life as the time to reach zero divided by 2.

mistakes.r: Corrected count rate = measured count rate - background count rate.
mistakes.w: Not subtracting background radiation from readings.

mistakes.r: Show construction lines and check that successive halving times are equal.
mistakes.w: Reading half-life from the graph without construction lines or checking a second halving.

mistakes.r: Half-life is unaffected by physical or chemical conditions, because decay is a nuclear process.
mistakes.w: Saying a higher temperature or a chemical reaction will change the half-life.

mistakes.r: Decay is random; only the behaviour of a large number of nuclei can be predicted.
mistakes.w: Saying you can predict when one nucleus will decay.

mistakes.r: Always include units and convert so the time and half-life use the same unit.
mistakes.w: Forgetting units or mixing up units (e.g. hours and days).

mistakes.r: Activity is the decay rate of the source; count rate is what the detector records, which is lower.

summary: The specification asks you to know that radioactive decay is random, to define half-life in terms of nuclei or count rate/activity, and to determine half-life from a graph or table. Higher tier students must also calculate the net decline as a ratio after a given number of half-lives. It matters because half-life explains how long sources stay active and underpins nuclear safety and medical choices.

terms.d: The time it takes for the number of nuclei of the isotope in a sample to halve, or the time it takes for the count rate (or activity) from a sample to fall to half its initial level.
The random process in which an unstable nucleus emits radiation to become more stable.
Cannot be predicted: it is impossible to say when a particular nucleus will decay.
The rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays, measured in becquerel (Bq).
The unit of activity; 1 Bq is one decay per second.
The number of decays recorded per second or per minute by a detector.
A detector that detects ionising radiation; each particle or ray entering produces a pulse that is counted.
Radiation that is always present from natural and man-made sources, which must be subtracted from readings.
Measured count rate minus background count rate.
Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
A nucleus that has too much energy or the wrong balance of particles and may emit radiation.
A pattern in which the quantity falls by the same fraction in equal time intervals.
The overall fall in activity or count rate after a given number of half-lives.
Unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on or in other materials.
The new nucleus formed after radioactive decay.

worked.ans: Count rate after 24 hours = 40 counts/s; the ratio initial : final is 16 : 1.
worked.q: A radioactive source has an initial count rate of 640 counts/s and a half-life of 6 hours. Calculate the count rate after 24 hours and state the net decline as a ratio of initial to final. (4 marks, Higher)
steps: Ratio initial : final = 640 : 40 = 16 : 1 (which is 2 to the power 4 : 1).

worked.q: The count rate from a source falls from 1200 counts/min to 150 counts/min in 90 minutes. Background has already been subtracted. Calculate the half-life. (3 marks)
A student measures 420 counts/min at the start and 70 counts/min after 2 hours. The background count rate is 20 counts/min. Calculate the half-life. (4 marks)
